source.title: Redundancy and Concept Analysis for Code-trained Language Models
source.authors: Arushi Sharma; Zefu Hu; Christopher J. Quinn; Ali Jannesari

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies neurons in code-trained models, but it does not test any listed version: it does not estimate the stated shares of neuron jobs, test the cited vision examples or estimates, build attribution graphs, or evaluate explanations on held-out activating examples or new text.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron-removal results and examples of neurons associated with code-token concepts. These bear on neuron-level analysis generally, but not on the specific measurements or tests named in V1–V7. It also discusses monosemanticity, polysemanticity and superposition; those discussions are not tests of the listed claims.
record.test_reason: The study probes code-trained models with LCA, correlation clustering, layer selection and CKA, and reports how many neurons can be removed while keeping probe accuracy. It inspects a handful of hand-picked neurons (top-5 words, NeuroX visualisations). It reports no share of neurons with one, two or no jobs (V1, V2). It does not address InceptionV1 or recursive generalization (V3), or tool/architecture-driven interpretability shares (V4). It builds no attribution graphs (V5). It does not test explanations on held-out firing (V6) or simulate activations (V7). The few neuron anecdotes are illustrative selections, not a rate, so they cannot bear on any version's share.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that most neurons (over 95%) are redundant for their code tasks and that small neuron subsets match or exceed oracle probe accuracy. Neurons can be traced to concepts such as number, string and text neurons. Superposition, possible shortcuts and probing confounders limit mechanistic conclusions. They explicitly leave superposition analysis out of scope.
record.recipe_differences: Uses probing classifiers, LCA, correlation clustering, layer selection and activation similarity analysis on code-trained models; it does not use the neuron-explanation evaluation procedure described by the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes vary by model, task and neuron-selection method; it also notes task-dependent differences in layer similarity and neuron reduction.

fits_no_version.finding: Over 95% of neurons can be removed with little or no loss in probe accuracy across seven code models and four tasks. Some reduced sets exceed the all-neuron probe; for example, CodeGPTPy token tagging reaches 87.84% with 49 neurons versus 80.25% with 9984.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-relevant information in code-trained LMs is concentrated in a small subset of neurons recoverable by probe-based ranking.

fits_no_version.finding: Hand-picked neurons include a clean 'number' neuron and neurons the authors call polysemantic or possibly superposed. No frequency of either kind is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual code-model neurons can be traced to token classes, with some mixed-concept neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: 2024 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering Workshops (ASEW)
record.problems: The authors note that results may not generalize to other code-related tasks; probing accuracy depends on the dataset, model, probing set and probing model; and neuron-ranking methods may not be optimal. The paper also says its findings do not establish whether models rely on shortcuts. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the recorded results.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 4 and 5 report many model-by-task-by-selection-method neuron counts and probing scores. They are not included because they concern task-specific probe performance and redundancy rather than any measurement named by V1–V7; the paper's aggregate result and an explicit reduced-set example are retained in R1–R2.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no shares of neuron poles by number of jobs.
No job-share distributions across models or scale. The models are small BERT/GPT2-sized code models and no share is reported.
No vision models, no InceptionV1 cat/car neuron, no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No measurement of interpretable-neuron share as a function of tools or architecture.
No attribution graphs or circuit-level explanation.
No test of whether explanations from activating examples predict firing elsewhere.

record.verdict_notes: The study discusses monosemantic and polysemantic neurons only by example, using Gurnee et al.'s definitions, and makes no quantitative interpretability-share claim. It is not an original source. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or report shares of positive or negative neuron poles by number of jobs.
Does not estimate job-share distributions across models, dense or mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter models.
Does not analyze InceptionV1's cat-and-car example or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not test the stated architecture/tool explanation or estimate interpretability shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain model behavior without a replacement model and reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations fit to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: seven code-trained language models (aggregate; individual models not specified in this reported result)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained models; sentence-level models were fine-tuned for downstream tasks
rows.operation_detail: Eliminated neurons judged similar or irrelevant to the task and assessed probing accuracy.
rows.measure: Neuron reduction without significant loss in probing accuracy
rows.baseline: probing classifier using all neurons (oracle accuracy)
rows.value: over 95% of neurons can be eliminated without significant loss in accuracy
rows.note: This is the authors' aggregate statement; detailed results are also reported separately in Tables 4 and 5.
rows.check: Redundancy result (probe accuracy after neuron removal); it is not a measure of neuron interpretability shares. The state 'observed' has no version to be observed against.

rows.subject: CodeGPTPy
rows.operation_detail: Selected a reduced neuron set using layer selection, correlation clustering and LCA, then evaluated a probing classifier.
rows.note: The table reports a 7.59% accuracy difference and 99.51% neuron reduction.
rows.check: This is a selection-method outcome (the study's own LS+CC+LCA reduced set versus the all-neuron probe), not a measure tied to any version.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Examined a neuron's activations for token classes using the NeuroX visualization tool.
rows.value: The neuron activates for identifiers and numbers, with negative activation values for identifiers and positive values for numbers.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a polysemantic neuron responsible for multiple concepts.
rows.check: A single hand-picked neuron anecdote with no rate, so it cannot inform the share-based versions. Its state relative to a version cannot be set.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Examined a neuron's activation examples for token classes using the NeuroX visualization tool.
rows.value: Primarily associated with strings, with a parenthesis also highlighted.
rows.note: The authors say the parenthesis may indicate polysemanticity or noise.
rows.check: A single hand-picked neuron anecdote. The reader's 'partial' state has no version referent.

rows.subject: CodeGPTPython
rows.operation_detail: Identified a high-ranking neuron for a token class using LCA and inspected its top words.
rows.value: Top words: 79, 104, 78, 118, 99; described as the cleanest example of a number neuron found.
rows.note: The paper does not report a share of neurons with this property.
rows.check: The authors call it the cleanest example found, which is a selection, not a share.

rows.subject: CodeGPTJava
rows.operation_detail: Identified a high-ranking neuron for token classes using LCA and inspected its top words.
rows.value: Associated with both keywords and identifiers.
rows.note: The authors suggest this could indicate superposition or be interpreted as a higher-level text neuron.
rows.check: A single anecdote that the authors themselves read ambiguously (superposition or higher-level text neuron).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
